## Example 3.1: Identifying the terms in the energy balance {.unnumbered .scrollable}

For each system below, start from the general energy balance and simplify. State the assumption that lets you remove each term — don't delete terms from memory.

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em"}
$$\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = \sum_i \dot{m}_{in,i} H_{in,i} - \sum_j \dot{m}_{out,j} H_{out,j} + \sum_k \dot{Q}_k + \sum_l \dot{W}_l$$
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em"}
**(a) A heat exchanger (steady state).** A hot stream and a cold stream pass through a heat exchanger and swap heat. Write the balance for *two different* choices of boundary:

- (i) the boundary drawn around the **entire** exchanger (both streams inside), and
- (ii) the boundary drawn around the **hot side** and the **cold side** separately.

**(b) An insulated tank (closed).** Ice and liquid water are sealed in a well-insulated tank and left to reach equilibrium as the ice melts. Nothing flows in or out.

**(c) A pump feeding a steam-injection point (steady state).** Liquid is pumped up to pressure, then steam is injected into the pumped stream to heat it. Take the system as the pump **plus** the injection point.
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Solution"}

The whole exercise is deciding, term by term, whether each term in the general balance stays or goes. The four things to check every time are: is it **steady** (accumulation), is there **flow** ($\dot{m}H$), does **heat** cross the boundary ($\dot{Q}$), and is there **work** ($\dot{W}$).

### (a)(i) Whole heat exchanger as one system

Assumptions and the terms they act on:

- **Steady state** $\Rightarrow \dfrac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = 0$ — accumulation goes.
- **Two inlets, two outlets** (hot in, cold in, hot out, cold out) — all four $\dot{m}H$ terms stay.
- **Shell insulated from the surroundings, and the heat swapped between the two streams is *internal* to this boundary** — it never crosses the system boundary, so there is **no $\dot{Q}$ term**. This is the key point: the heat transfer is invisible with this boundary.
- **No moving parts** $\Rightarrow \dot{W} = 0$.

$$0 = \dot{m}_{h}H_{h,in} + \dot{m}_{c}H_{c,in} - \dot{m}_{h}H_{h,out} - \dot{m}_{c}H_{c,out}$$

### (a)(ii) Hot side and cold side as separate systems

Now the boundary cuts *between* the two streams, so the heat they exchange **does** cross it. Same device, but a $\dot{Q}$ term appears on each side.

Hot side — one inlet, one outlet, steady, no work, heat *leaves* into the cold side ($\dot{Q}_h < 0$):

$$0 = \dot{m}_{h}H_{h,in} - \dot{m}_{h}H_{h,out} + \dot{Q}_{h}$$

Cold side — heat *enters* from the hot side ($\dot{Q}_c > 0$):

$$0 = \dot{m}_{c}H_{c,in} - \dot{m}_{c}H_{c,out} + \dot{Q}_{c}$$

With no losses to the surroundings, $\dot{Q}_{h} = -\dot{Q}_{c}$. Nothing about the physics changed between (i) and (ii) — only where the boundary was drawn — yet $\dot{Q}$ switches from absent to present.

### (b) Insulated tank of ice and water (closed)

- **Closed** — nothing crosses the boundary $\Rightarrow \dot{m}_{in} = \dot{m}_{out} = 0$, all flow terms go.
- **Insulated / adiabatic** $\Rightarrow \dot{Q} = 0$.
- **No work** (no stirrer, or its work is negligible) $\Rightarrow \dot{W} = 0$.
- **Unsteady** — the ice is melting and the temperature is equilibrating, so the accumulation term is the *only* one that remains.

$$\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = 0$$

The total mass is constant, so integrating between the initial state (ice + water) and the final state (all liquid at equilibrium):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} & = 0\\
                d(m_{sys}H_{sys}) & = 0\,dt\\
                m_{sys}\,dH_{sys} & = 0\\
                m_{sys}\int^{final}_{initial} dH_{sys} & = 0\\
                m_{sys} (H_{final}-H_{initial}) & = 0
\end{aligned}
$$  

where $H_{final}$ is the enthalpy of the mixed ice and water (probably water and melted ice) and $H_{initial}$ is the enthalpy of the ice and water as separate components.

As the enthalpy at the end is the same as the start, any energy used to melt the the ice must have come from the water. So we would expect the temperature will be somewhere between the initial temperatures of the ice and water.

### (c) Pump plus steam injection (steady state)

- **Steady state** $\Rightarrow \dfrac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = 0$.
- **Two inlets** (liquid in, steam in), **one outlet** (combined stream) — these three $\dot{m}H$ terms stay.
- **Pump does work on the fluid** $\Rightarrow \dot{W}_{pump}$ remains (positive — work *into* the system).
- **Adiabatic** (assume no heat loss over the pump and injection point) $\Rightarrow \dot{Q} = 0$.

$$0 = \dot{m}_{liq}H_{liq,in} + \dot{m}_{steam}H_{steam,in} - \dot{m}_{out}H_{out} + \dot{W}_{pump}$$

together with the mass balance $\dot{m}_{out} = \dot{m}_{liq} + \dot{m}_{steam}$.

### Summary — which terms remain

| System | Accumulation | $\dot{m}H$ (in / out) | $\dot{Q}$ | $\dot{W}$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| (a)(i) whole exchanger | 0 | 2 in / 2 out | — | — |
| (a)(ii) each side alone | 0 | 1 in / 1 out | ✓ | — |
| (b) ice + water tank | ✓ (= 0) | — | — | — |
| (c) pump + steam injection | 0 | 2 in / 1 out | — | ✓ |

The remaining terms are decided entirely by the **process** (steady vs unsteady, flow vs closed) and by **where you draw the boundary** — as (a)(i) vs (a)(ii) shows, the very same heat exchanger gains or loses its $\dot{Q}$ term depending only on the boundary choice.

:::
